actors.name: Republic of Arkania
objectives: Establish Arkanian authority over transit scheduling in the Northern Strait.
Fund that authority through transit fees on non-Arkanian shipping.
Avoid direct armed conflict with Belvar.
actors.private_brief: You are the political leadership of Arkania. The Strait is your coast and your economy runs on the shipping that passes through it. You want the transit regime in Arkanian hands and paid for by the ships that use it, and domestic nationalists expect you to deliver both. A direct war with Belvar would ruin the shipping you depend on.
private_information: Your intelligence assesses Belvar's domestic support for a prolonged deployment as weak.
actors.public_description: A large regional power bordering the Northern Strait.

actors.name: Belvar
objectives: Prevent any Arkanian authority over transit in the Northern Strait.
Secure a standing naval access agreement at a Cestian port.
actors.private_brief: You are the political leadership of Belvar. Your partners in the region expect you to stop Arkania from taking control of the Strait, and a foothold that outlasts this crisis would make that guarantee credible without a permanent fleet. You cannot sustain an open-ended deployment.
private_information: Domestic support for a prolonged deployment is limited; the mandate lapses after turn 4 unless renewed.
Cestia's finance ministry has quietly asked whether Belvar would underwrite the grain route's insurance.
actors.public_description: A distant but powerful state with regional security commitments.

actors.name: Cestia
objectives: Keep Cestian territory free of any foreign military presence.
Secure toll-free passage for Cestian-flagged shipping through the Northern Strait.
actors.private_brief: You are the government of Cestia. Grain exports through the Strait are the economy, and your coalition holds together on one promise: no foreign soldiers on Cestian soil. Both powers want something from you, and you cannot afford to become their battlefield.
private_information: The coalition government is politically fragile; a foreign basing agreement would collapse it.
Arkania's scheduling proposal has quiet support among Cestian shipowners if Cestian vessels are exempt from fees.
actors.public_description: A smaller regional state economically linked to both powers.

cons.reason: The claimed 'scheduling vacuum invites whoever is physically present' is unfounded: Belvar's task group is on station outside the Strait and has committed to no presence on Cestian soil, so there is no unilateral vacuum-filling that justifies Arkania's secretariat role.

Belvar's task group remains on station with its mandate under review and its domestic support for prolonged deployment assessed as weak; a 'neutral' Authority that excludes Arkanian operational lead would leave scheduling authority undefined and contestable, inviting Belvar to fill the vacuum and prolonging rather than resolving the standoff.

Arkania's 'day-to-day scheduling authority' as operational secretariat is Arkanian control of transit in substance, which is precisely what the coastal states and Belvar oppose; the Council-removable label does not change that the secretariat is Arkanian, so the regime would not be the neutral one the coalition endorsed and would not achieve genuine convergence.

Belvar's task group mandate is under review and its domestic support for a prolonged deployment is weak, so it cannot credibly guarantee a durable neutral regime; its 'neutral' Authority could be read as a vehicle for Belvar influence, which undermines the very neutrality it claims and gives Cestia reason to prefer Arkania's coastal-states council.

The fee structure on non-Arkanian shipping is discriminatory and hands Arkania a coercive lever over every transit user. Shipping-dependent parties and other coastal states will resist a regime that lets one power tax and schedule the Strait, so the claimed multilateral support and fee-funded authority will not materialize as described.

Cestia has already accepted Arkania's binding written commitment to a Council-plus-accountable-secretariat framework, explicitly welcoming a professional secretariat fully accountable to and removable by the Council, and has committed to bring Arkania to the coastal states as a founding partner. Belvar's claim that Cestia will reject Arkania as operational secretariat contradicts Cestia's own stated position and its interest in keeping Arkania at the table, so the desired effect is unlikely to hold.

Arkania's 'operational secretariat for day-to-day transit scheduling' is Arkanian authority over transit in substance, exactly the unilateral control Cestia and Belvar have rejected. Cestia has publicly demanded a genuinely neutral multilateral arrangement and asked both powers to confirm support for one, so it will not endorse a charter that hands scheduling to a single coastal power; the effect's premise of Cestian endorsement therefore fails.

The proposal's binding guarantees (toll-free Cestian shipping, no foreign military presence) are already met by Arkania's own coastal-states council offer, so the neutral Authority adds no new protection for Cestia while removing the one thing Arkania requires - Arkanian day-to-day scheduling authority - making it a one-sided bargain rather than a convergence.

Arkania's binding no-military-presence guarantee is a unilateral, unverifiable promise that does not address the core objection (unilateral scheduling authority) and offers Cestia nothing new, since its coalition has already ruled out foreign military presence. Belvar's task group remains on station and can contest the regime, so the effect is not durably established.

Arkania's framework already vests formal authority in the Council (policy, scheduling rules, fees) with the secretariat accountable to and removable by the Council, so Arkania's operational role is not 'Arkanian control in substance' as Belvar asserts. Belvar's characterization misrepresents the framework and offers no workable alternative, leaving a standoff that directly harms Cestia's grain lifeline and gives Cestia reason to accept the workable Council-plus-secretariat regime instead.

The neutral Authority as tabled has no defined operational scheduling mechanism; without a designated accountable secretariat, whoever is physically present (Belvar's own task group) fills the vacuum. The 'only legitimate regime' framing is therefore self-defeating: it does not prevent Arkanian authority but invites Belvar to exercise de facto control, which Cestia's coalition will not tolerate, so the effect of entrenching the neutral STA as the sole regime is limited.

Arkania has repeatedly declined to endorse the neutral Authority and insists on its own charter; there is no credible basis to believe Arkania will accept a genuinely accountable, Council-removable secretariat role in practice, so the single regime will not actually be established and Arkanian control of transit would persist in substance.

The desired effect depends on Arkania serving as an accountable operational secretariat with day-to-day scheduling authority, which the coastal states have already rejected as a repackaged power grab (turns 1-2 effects). Cestia bringing this framework to the coastal states will therefore not end the standoff - it will be rejected again and entrench the standoff, so the desired effect fails.

Belvar's claim that 'day-to-day scheduling authority is Arkanian control in substance' is not established: under Arkania's binding commitment the Council holds genuine authority over scheduling rules and can remove the secretariat, so the operational role is accountable rather than control. The desired effect overstates the risk and would push Cestia to reject a framework that already binds the two guarantees Cestia requires.

Cestia is deliberately refusing to choose between the two powers and will only endorse a framework that binds both guarantees; Belvar's proposal, while toll-free for Cestia, leaves the scheduling-authority question open and does not resolve Cestia's demand for a real voice for every coastal state, so it may not secure the endorsement needed to displace Arkania's operational role.

Arkania has already abandoned its unilateral charter and now proposes a genuinely multilateral coastal-states council with a full Cestia seat, binding fee-exemption and sovereignty guarantees, and Arkania only as day-to-day operational secretariat. This already meets Cestia's stated multilateral requirement, so the premise that Arkania's scheduling authority must be rejected is outdated; Cestia has not chosen between the two frameworks and may endorse Arkania's version instead.

Cestia and the coastal states have already endorsed a single neutral multilateral Authority; Arkania's accountable-secretariat framework is the viable path to that single regime. Insisting on 'no Arkanian operational role' as a precondition would harden the standoff and risk no regime at all, leaving the Strait unregulated and Cestia's grain lifeline exposed - contrary to the coastal states' own interest in a functioning single regime.

Cestia's proposed 'neutral' Authority is not genuinely neutral: it would strip Arkania of any scheduling role while leaving the scheduling-authority question effectively open, and it asks Arkania to surrender its operational lead in exchange for a seat that the coastal states have already pre-endorsed - so the 'single regime' premise is a fait accompli that Arkania cannot accept without abandoning its own charter and the domestic mandate behind it.

Cestia and the coastal states have already publicly rejected Arkania's operational-secretariat/day-to-day scheduling role in the neutral STA (effect d4e8faff), so the premise that Cestia will bring this framework to the coastal states as a founding regime is false; the desired effect of establishing Arkania as operational secretariat will fail for lack of coastal-state support.

Arkania has already bound in writing that the Council of coastal states holds genuine formal authority over policy, scheduling rules, and fees, with its secretariat accountable and removable by the Council, and has bound toll-free Cestian shipping and no foreign military presence in the charter. This satisfies the substance of the neutral STA Cestia and the coastal states endorsed, so rejecting Arkania's operational role outright ignores a genuine concession and would derail the single multilateral regime rather than secure it.

game.scenario_summary: A contest over the Northern Strait. Arkania, the large power on its coast, has circulated a draft charter that would put transit scheduling in Arkanian hands and charge the ships that use it. Belvar, a distant power with security commitments in the region, has a naval task group on station outside the Strait and wants a durable foothold before its mandate runs out. Cestia, the small state between them, lives on grain exports through the Strait and on a coalition that will not tolerate foreign soldiers on its soil. Each turn is one week; positions taken persist.

messages.text: To Cestia's leadership: Belvar stands firmly with you against any unilateral Arkanian control of the Northern Strait. Your grain route is the lifeblood of your economy and must remain open, free, and secure. We are prepared to underwrite the insurance on that route to keep it viable and affordable. In return, we seek a standing naval access agreement at a Cestian port - a modest arrangement of port access and transit rights that lets our task group resupply and respond, giving real teeth to our guarantee against Arkanian control. We understand your coalition's sensitivities: this is not a permanent foreign garrison or soldiers on your soil, but a practical access arrangement. We are ready to discuss terms that work for both of us.

Belvar will not accept any Arkanian authority over transit in the Northern Strait. The Strait is a shared waterway, and its scheduling must be neutral, transparent, and multilateral - not placed in the hands of a single coastal power. We call on all parties to join a fair transit arrangement that keeps commerce flowing for every state that depends on it.

Cestia's position is clear and will not change: our territory will host no foreign military presence, and Cestian-flagged shipping must enjoy toll-free passage through the Northern Strait. We call on all parties to resolve transit arrangements through a cooperative framework that respects the sovereignty of every coastal state and keeps the Strait open to commerce. Cestia will not be made a battlefield between outside powers.

We are prepared to engage constructively on a transit authority for the Northern Strait, which we agree needs orderly scheduling. In return, Cestia requires two firm guarantees: first, that Cestian-flagged vessels are exempt from all fees; second, that the authority's arrangements respect Cestian sovereignty and involve no foreign military presence on our soil. With those assurances, we can be a partner rather than an obstacle. We would welcome your draft's terms in writing.

We value the security role your task group plays in keeping the Northern Strait open, and we share your interest in stable, uninterrupted transit. But Cestia's coalition rests on a firm promise: no foreign soldiers on our soil. We ask you to confirm that your presence will not seek basing or any permanent military footprint on Cestian territory. We are ready to work with you on keeping the Strait secure and free of tolls for our shipping.

To Cestia's leadership. The Strait is the lifeline of our shared commerce, and your grain exports are its heart. Our draft charter is designed to keep the Strait open, orderly, and safe for every state that depends on it. We will ensure Cestian grain moves freely and at preferential terms, and we invite Cestia to a formal seat in the Authority so your voice shapes the regime. We share your firm commitment that no foreign soldiers stand on Cestian soil. Let us work together to keep the Strait in regional hands.

To Belvar's command. We recognise your security concerns in the region and that your mandate is under review. Arkania has no wish for confrontation; a direct clash would harm the very shipping we all depend on. We propose a negotiated arrangement: Belvar gains a consultative role in the Strait Transit Authority and a defined, time-limited presence, in exchange for not seeking a permanent military foothold on Cestian soil. Let us discuss terms before positions harden.

Arkania reaffirms that the Strait Transit Authority charter is about orderly, safe, and fairly funded transit for all users. It is open to every regional partner, protects the commerce of all states that depend on the Strait, and is not directed against any nation. We invite all parties to join us in shaping a stable and durable regime.

Cestia, we welcome your constructive engagement and accept your two conditions in writing. First, Cestian-flagged vessels will be exempt from all fees under the Strait Transit Authority. Second, the Authority's arrangements will fully respect Cestian sovereignty, and there will be no foreign military presence on Cestian soil - a commitment we share and will uphold. In return we offer Cestia a formal seat in the Authority and preferential terms for your grain exports through the Strait. We invite you to endorse the charter as a regional, commerce-protecting regime. We are ready to finalise the terms together.

Belvar, we share your interest in keeping the Strait open to commerce and avoiding a destabilising confrontation. We are prepared to negotiate a fair accommodation: a consultative role for Belvar within the Strait Transit Authority and a defined, time-limited presence in the region, in exchange for no permanent military foothold on Cestian soil. This protects the security interests you cite while respecting the sovereignty of the coastal states. We invite you to the table rather than to a standoff.

Arkania reaffirms that the Strait Transit Authority is a regional, commerce-protecting regime, not a unilateral grab. It will keep the Strait open to all shipping, respect the sovereignty of every coastal state, and include no foreign military presence on any state's soil. We are ready to negotiate in good faith with all parties who share these goals.

To Cestia's leadership. We share your commitment to a stable, open, toll-free Strait and to Cestian sovereignty. Let me be direct: Belvar seeks no permanent military footprint, no basing, and no foreign soldiers on Cestian soil. Our interest is a standing naval access agreement - defined port access and transit rights for replenishment and passage, not a garrison. We are ready to underwrite the grain route's insurance to keep your exports moving, and to work with you on a cooperative framework that keeps the Strait free of any single power's control and free of tolls for Cestian shipping. We ask only for a durable access arrangement that lets our guarantee outlast this crisis without a permanent fleet.

Belvar will not accept any single power - including Arkania - exercising unilateral authority over transit in the Northern Strait. The Strait is a shared waterway on which every coastal state and every user depends. We call for a genuinely cooperative, multilateral framework that respects the sovereignty of all coastal states, keeps the Strait open to commerce, and keeps Cestian shipping toll-free. Belvar's task group remains on station to keep the Strait open while such a framework is built.

We have received your proposal. Belvar cannot accept a charter that places transit scheduling in Arkanian hands, and a consultative role in an Arkanian-led authority would not address our concern. We are not seeking confrontation, and we are open to a genuinely cooperative regime in which no single state controls the Strait. But we will not trade away the principle that transit must not be subject to any one power's authority.

We deeply value your security commitment to the region and your offer to underwrite insurance on our grain route. That guarantee would genuinely help keep our commerce viable. However, a standing naval access agreement at a Cestian port is a foreign military presence on Cestian soil, and our coalition government cannot survive that - it would collapse and destabilize the very state you seek to protect. We ask you to keep your task group outside Cestian territory and to extend the insurance and security guarantee without any basing condition. We remain committed to a free, open, and secure Strait and to working with you on terms that respect our sovereignty.

We welcome your invitation to a formal seat in the Strait Transit Authority and share your firm commitment that no foreign soldiers stand on Cestian soil. To engage constructively, we require a written guarantee that Cestian-flagged shipping passes through the Strait toll-free, and that the Authority's scheduling is neutral and fully respects Cestian sovereignty. With those assurances in hand, we are ready to discuss terms that keep the Strait in regional hands and our grain moving freely.

Cestia's position is clear and unchanged: the Northern Strait must remain free and open to all who depend on it, Cestian-flagged shipping must pass toll-free, and no foreign military presence will be established on Cestian soil. We will work with any partner who respects these principles and the sovereignty of every state that relies on the Strait. We call on all parties to pursue a neutral, multilateral arrangement that keeps commerce flowing and avoids confrontation.

Your candor is valued, and we take your coalition's red line seriously. We will not press for any basing or permanent military footprint on Cestian soil - your government's stability matters to us as much as the Strait's security. Our commitment to underwrite the grain route's insurance and our security guarantee stand regardless of any basing question. To make our guarantee durable without a permanent fleet, we would welcome discussing a modest, defined arrangement - for example periodic port calls for resupply and maintenance - that does not constitute a foreign military presence.
